title: A Gene of the Birds Themselves

scenes.tts: Where did a virus get a cancer gene? In San Francisco, Michael Bishop and Harold Varmus shared a laboratory. A French postdoctoral fellow there, Dominique Stehelin, made a radioactive strand of D N A. It matched the sark gene and no other part of the virus. A single strand of D N A sticks to its matching sequence. So this probe could ask whether any sample of D N A held a relative of sark.
scenes.caption: Where did a virus get a cancer gene? In San Francisco, Michael Bishop and Harold Varmus shared a laboratory. A French postdoctoral fellow there, Dominique Stehelin, made a radioactive strand of DNA. It matched the src gene and no other part of the virus. A single strand of DNA sticks to its matching sequence. So this probe could ask whether any sample of DNA held a relative of src.
scenes.visual: Virus bar with a toothed src segment; Stehelin's probe strand with matching teeth docks on src only and bounces off other segments; then a question-mark DNA sample box.
scenes.narration: Where did a virus get a cancer gene? In San Francisco, Michael Bishop and Harold Varmus shared a laboratory. A French postdoctoral fellow there, Dominique Stehelin, made a radioactive strand of DNA. It matched the src gene and no other part of the virus. A single strand of DNA sticks to its matching sequence. So this probe could ask whether any sample of DNA held a relative of src.

scenes.tts: The probe stuck to D N A from chickens that had never met the virus. That alone proved little. A leading idea of the day held that old infections had left viral genes behind in chicken chromosomes. So a match in chickens could still be a leftover from an old infection.
scenes.caption: The probe stuck to DNA from chickens that had never met the virus. That alone proved little. A leading idea of the day held that old infections had left viral genes behind in chicken chromosomes. So a match in chickens could still be a leftover from an old infection.
scenes.visual: Probe docks on a chicken DNA bar; stuck. Then an old-infection virus chip with an arrow into the chicken DNA, tagged as the leading idea of the day, and a question mark.
scenes.narration: The probe stuck to DNA from chickens that had never met the virus. That alone proved little. A leading idea of the day held that old infections had left viral genes behind in chicken chromosomes. So a match in chickens could still be a leftover from an old infection.

scenes.tts: So Stehelin tried duck, quail and emu. An emu is a flightless bird at a great evolutionary distance from the chicken. The probe stuck to all of them. The matches were close enough that Varmus judged the sequence had been conserved for at least 100 million years. A sequence shared across that distance is older than any infection of chickens.

scenes.tts: It was a gene of the birds themselves. Later work found it in mammals, people included. The virus had picked up the cell's gene by accident. A normal gene that can become an oncogene when it is altered is a proto-oncogene. What the virus carries now is an altered copy.
